own_scenes.family: Old school: DJs, MCs y fiestas del Bronx
own_scenes.desc: Tras varias formaciones, DJ Charlie Chase y Tony Tone reunieron en una audición del instituto South Bronx a Easy A.D., Almighty Kay Gee, Grandmaster Caz (antes DJ Casanova Fly) y JDL, al que Caz impuso pese a su fama de salvaje. Ensayaban de seis a ocho horas al día. Pioneros del marketing: Elvis «Tape Master» Moreno grababa sus actuaciones directamente de la mesa, Joe Conzo las fotografiaba y Buddy Esquire dibujaba sus flyers; sus cintas llegaron a bases militares de Alemania o Japón («nunca prestes tu cinta de los Cold Crush») y Russell Simmons obligaba a Run-DMC a escucharlas cada día. En la batalla del Harlem World del 3 de julio de 1981, con trajes de gánster, fedoras y pistolas de plástico, perdieron contra los Fantastic Five, pero las grabaciones los consagraron como el grupo más selecto de la ciudad: hip hop en su forma más cruda, MCs que iban a destruir a los otros MCs.

influences.name: Las crews de MCs: Funky 4 + 1, Treacherous Three, Fantastic Five
Grandmaster Flash y el arte del DJ

refs.q: We was our own media, our own flyer distribution, our own sound people, so we did everything.
refs.para: Easy A.D. (Cold Crush Brothers): We was our own media, our own flyer distribution, our own sound people, so we did everything.

refs.q: I tell people, that’s the night I was kidnapped by the culture of hip-hop.
refs.para: I landed at the T-Connection one Friday night. I took pictures of the Cold Crush Brothers playing music that I’d never heard played that way. Charlie Chase was playing Aretha Franklin and James Brown, all this music that I grew up on from my parents, but he wasn’t playing it the way I was used to hearing it played. I tell people, that’s the night I was kidnapped by the culture of hip-hop.

refs.q: Don’t never lend your Cold Crush tape out, because you ain’t going to get it back.
refs.para: Easy A.D. (Cold Crush Brothers): One of the things that I really like about what we did is our tapes went from New York City to Florida to Germany to Japan, so it went to all the military bases around the world where people had their brothers and sisters in the military. One of the other things people used to say: “Don’t never lend your Cold Crush tape out, because you ain’t going to get it back.”

refs.q: What I liked about Cold Crush, they didn’t need to have successful records because they kept hip-hop to its rawest form.
refs.para: DMC (artist, Run-DMC): When I first heard the Cold Crush, it was different hip-hop because it was the first time where the MCs were actually going at the other MCs with a destroying attitude. They made it all about the performance and presentation of the DJ and MC. All the beats that Charlie Chase and Tony Tone was choosing precisely fit the attitude and the vibe of each routine. What I liked about Cold Crush, they didn’t need to have successful records because they kept hip-hop to its rawest form.
